about.title: Millbrae Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Millbrae's mix of retail strips along El Camino Real, residential complexes near the BART/Caltrain hub, and commercial buildings off US-101 means falls happen in a variety of settings — wet tile in a grocery store, a broken stair rail at an apartment building, uneven pavement in a parking lot. California law requires showing the property owner or manager knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn visitors. That's why what happens right after a fall matters: photos of the spill, torn carpet, or missing signage, plus witness names, can make a real difference weeks later. Surveillance footage at many Millbrae businesses is often overwritten within days or weeks, so acting quickly to request preservation is important. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we connect injured Millbrae residents with an independent attorney, free of charge, who can evaluate the specifics of where and how the fall happened.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Millbrae Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Key Legal Question
items.desc: California requires proof the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney knows how to gather maintenance logs, inspection records, and prior complaints to establish that notice.

items.title: Video Evidence Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Millbrae businesses and apartment complexes recycle surveillance footage within days. A quick attorney-issued preservation request can stop that footage from being erased before it's reviewed.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Bar, Recovery
items.desc: Even if a property owner argues you weren't watching where you stepped, California's pure comparative fault rule still allows partial recovery based on the percentage of fault assigned to each side.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Millbrae?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity — a city building, transit station, or public sidewalk — the deadline is much shorter and requires a formal claim first. It's worth having an attorney check this early.

items.question: What if I fell at a business near El Camino Real or the BART station?
items.answer: High-traffic commercial corridors like El Camino Real see heavier foot traffic, which can mean more frequent spills, debris, or maintenance gaps. An attorney can request the store's or property manager's maintenance and cleaning records to see if the hazard existed long enough that staff should have caught it.

items.question: Do I need proof the owner knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Yes, generally you need to show the property owner or manager either knew about the dangerous condition or should have discovered it through reasonable inspection. This is often the most contested part of a premises liability case. Documentation like photos, witness statements, and surveillance video helps build that case.
